At the end of the street stood a repair shop for things that were not quite broken.

Its window displayed a clock that ran correctly but made every hour feel like a deadline, a kettle whose whistle reminded its owner of an argument, and a pair of shoes that had become difficult to wear after a journey home.

The proprietor was a quiet woman with excellent tools.

People often arrived embarrassed.

“It still works,” they would say, placing an object on the counter.

“Of course,” she would answer.

One afternoon, a boy brought her a small blue cup.

“What seems to be the trouble?”

“My brother moved away,” he said.

She examined the cup. There was a chip in the rim, but it was old and smooth.

“Did he drink from this?”

“No. I did. He had the green one.”

The woman nodded. She took the cup to her workbench and returned with it wrapped in paper.

“What did you do?” the boy asked.

“Nothing yet. Take it home. Ask your brother what he drinks from now.”

The boy looked doubtful, but he took the parcel.

A week later, the woman saw him passing the shop with a green cup in his hand. He stopped to show her. It was new, taller than the blue one, with a badly painted fox on its side.

“He says this is the closest I could get here.”

“Will you send it to him?”

The boy shook his head.

“This one’s mine. He bought two.”
